```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(googlesheets4)

gs4_deauth()

sheet_url <- "https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1e0eL4NFmGThSgUOGeWmG45urZGSrfKUgX-94tiZ6j6A/edit#gid=1253615536"

# Columns by position: C = value of X, E = estimated % of US bird species in CA
birds <- read_sheet(sheet_url) |>
  select(anchor = 3, ca_pct = 5, prior_know = 6) |>
  mutate(
    anchor = factor(anchor, levels = c(50, 70)),
    ca_pct = as.numeric(ca_pct),
    prior_know = as.numeric(prior_know)
  )

set.seed(222)
theme_set(theme_bw(18))
```

# American birds revisited

## American birds, visualized

Here's the data from the classroom experiment. Use these data to complete the worksheet.

```{r}
ggplot(birds, aes(x = prior_know, y = ca_pct, shape = anchor)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("circle filled", "triangle filled")) +
  labs(x = "Prior Knowledge", y = "% American \nBirds in CA", shape = "Anchor")
```

## Interpreting multiple predictors

A coefficient estimate is the effect of the predictor _**when holding all else equal**_

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

```{r}
#| echo: true

american_birds_lm <- lm(ca_pct ~ anchor + prior_know, birds)
summary(american_birds_lm)
```

:::

## Multiple regression is _additive_

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}
$$
\begin{align}
\text{Perc. CA} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Prior knowledge} + \beta_2 {(Anchor=70)} + \epsilon \\
\epsilon &\sim Normal(0, \sigma)
\end{align}
$$
:::

```{r}
#| fig-align: center

model_grid <- expand_grid(prior_know = 0:12, anchor = factor(c(50, 70)))
model_pred <- model_grid |>
  mutate(ca_pct = predict(american_birds_lm, newdata = model_grid))
ggplot(birds, aes(x = prior_know, y = ca_pct, shape = anchor)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = anchor), model_pred) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("circle filled", "triangle filled")) +
  labs(
    x = "Prior Knowledge",
    y = "% American \nBirds in CA",
    shape = "Anchor",
    linetype = "Anchor"
  )
```

## American Bird DAG

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {"themeVariables": {"fontSize": "24px"}}}%%
flowchart LR
    n0((% American<br/>birds in CA))
    n1((Anchor))
    n2((Prior<br/>knowledge))
    n1 --> n0
    n2 --> n0
```

:::

::: {.column}

Why isn't there an arrow connecting _Anchor_ and _Prior knowledge_?


::: {.fragment}

Assignment of _Anchor_ was **randomized**. Intervening on _Anchor_ can have no effect on _Prior knowledge_ when their relationship is random.

:::


:::

:::

## Coefficient estimates unchanged

When predictors are _independent_, coefficient estimates don't affect each other. 

::: {.columns style="font-size: 0.8em"}

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| echo: true

two_predictors <- lm(
  ca_pct ~ anchor + prior_know,
  birds
)
coef(two_predictors)
summary(two_predictors)$r.squared
```

:::

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| echo: true

one_predictor <- lm(
  ca_pct ~ anchor,
  birds
)
coef(one_predictor)
summary(one_predictor)$r.squared
```

:::

:::

"Prior knowledge" _explained variance_, but the estimate for "Anchor" was unaffected.


## But observational data is messy

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

When predictors are dependent, their coefficients affect each other.

# Simpson's Paradox

## Simpson's paradox

> Simpson's paradox is a phenomenon in probability and statistics in which a trend appears in several groups of data but disappears or reverses when the groups are combined.

[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simpson%27s_paradox)

## How does bleaching respond to temperature?

```{r}
set.seed(123)
n_per_region <- 40
coral_params <- tibble(
  region = factor(
    c("Coolest", "Moderate", "Warmest"),
    levels = c("Coolest", "Moderate", "Warmest")
  ),
  sst_mean = c(28, 29, 30),
  region_effect = c(0, -20, -40)
)
beta_0 <- -151
beta_sst <- 8
sigma <- 5

coral <- coral_params |>
  slice(rep(1:3, each = n_per_region)) |>
  mutate(
    peak_sst = rnorm(n(), sst_mean, 0.5),
    percent_bleached = beta_0 +
      beta_sst * peak_sst +
      region_effect +
      rnorm(n(), 0, sigma)
  ) |>
  select(region, peak_sst, percent_bleached)
```

Each point is a coral reef. What's the relationship between temperature and bleaching?

```{r}
ggplot(coral, aes(peak_sst, percent_bleached)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Peak SST (degC)",
    y = "Percent bleached",
    caption = "Simulated data"
  )
```

## How about now?

How does bleaching respond to temperature?

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(coral, aes(peak_sst, percent_bleached)) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = region), shape = 21, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdYlBu", direction = -1) +
  labs(x = "Peak SST (degC)", y = "Percent bleached", fill = "Region") +
  theme(legend_position = "bottom")
```

::: {.fragment}
_**Regions**_ with _**higher temperatures**_ are associated with corals that are _**bleaching resistant**_
:::

Ignorning "Region" opens the door to **bias**.

## Coefficient reversal, visual

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6

model_levels <- c(
  "percent_bleached ~ peak_sst",
  "percent_bleached ~ peak_sst + region"
)
model_labels <- c(
  "Pooled",
  "Grouped"
)
pooled_lm <- lm(percent_bleached ~ peak_sst, coral)
region_lm <- lm(percent_bleached ~ peak_sst + region, coral)
coral_fits <- bind_rows(
  coral |>
    mutate(
      model = model_levels[1],
      fit = predict(pooled_lm),
      line_group = "All"
    ),
  coral |>
    mutate(
      model = model_levels[2],
      fit = predict(region_lm),
      line_group = region
    )
) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = model_levels, labels = model_labels))

ggplot(coral_fits, aes(peak_sst, percent_bleached)) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = region), shape = 21, color = "black", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit, group = line_group), linewidth = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdYlBu", direction = -1) +
  labs(x = "Peak SST (degC)", y = "Percent bleached", fill = "Region") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Coefficient reversal, numeric

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

two_predictors <- lm(percent_bleached ~ region + peak_sst, coral)
summary(two_predictors)
```

```r

```

```{r}
summary(one_predictor)
```

```r

peak_sst       -6.9329      0.9603 
```

# Recap

## Correlated predictors open the door to bias

```{r}
ggplot(coral_fits, aes(peak_sst, percent_bleached)) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = region), shape = 21, color = "black", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit, group = line_group), linewidth = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdYlBu", direction = -1) +
  labs(x = "Peak SST (degC)", y = "Percent bleached", fill = "Region") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Multiple regression adds predictors...

$$
\begin{align}
y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_n x_n + \epsilon \\
\epsilon &\sim Normal(0, \sigma)
\end{align}
$$

## ...which adjusts for bias

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

two_predictors <- lm(percent_bleached ~ region + peak_sst, coral)
summary(two_predictors)
```

```r

(Intercept)    -192.069     28.333
regionModerate  -20.797      1.478
regionWarmest   -42.284      2.286
peak_sst          9.447      1.011 
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

one_predictor <- lm(percent_bleached ~ peak_sst, coral)
summary(one_predictor)
```

